ai.title: Tramadol Analgesia
ai.subject: Pharmacology
ai.summary: Tramadol is a centrally acting analgesic with weak opioid activity and serotonin‑norepinephrine reuptake inhibition. It is used for moderate pain, especially where stronger opioids are unavailable or contraindicated.

b: Pro‑drug: metabolised by CYP2D6 to O‑desmethyltramadol (M1), the more potent µ‑agonist
sections.p: Tramadol is a synthetic analgesic that binds to µ‑opioid receptors and inhibits reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine, providing multimodal pain relief.

b: Risk of serotonin syndrome when combined with other serotonergic drugs
Lower respiratory depression risk than strong opioids, but still present
sections.p: Understanding tramadol requires knowledge of its dual mechanism, metabolism variability, and safety profile, especially in low‑resource settings where monitoring may be limited.

b: Preferred when opioid tolerance is low
Avoid in uncontrolled epilepsy (low seizure threshold)
Caution in HIV/TB patients on rifampicin (induces CYP2D6 → reduced effect)
sections.p: Tramadol is useful for postoperative pain, cancer‑related pain, and sickle‑cell crises where stronger opioids are scarce. It is contraindicated in severe renal/hepatic failure and in patients on MAO inhibitors.

t.b: Is dose adjustment needed? – Impaired clearance increases risk of accumulation and toxicity
Is metabolism likely reduced? – Hepatic dysfunction lowers conversion to active M1, altering efficacy
Is there a risk of serotonin syndrome? – Co‑administration with SSRIs, SNRIs, linezolid, or tramadol increases risk
Will patient be a poor or ultra‑rapid metaboliser? – Guides expectation of analgesic response

b: Analgesic ladder: non‑opioid → tramadol → stronger opioid
Add NSAID or paracetamol for multimodal effect if not contraindicated
Switch to stronger opioid if pain uncontrolled after adequate tramadol trial
sections.p: Start with the lowest effective dose, titrate to pain control, and monitor for side‑effects. Use adjuncts when pain is severe.

b: Unlike morphine, tramadol has lower respiratory depression risk but higher seizure risk
Codeine also requires CYP2D6 activation, but tramadol’s SNRI component makes serotonin syndrome a unique concern
sections.p: Tramadol may be mistaken for stronger opioids (morphine, fentanyl) or for non‑opioid analgesics like codeine.

b: Normal respiratory rate can mask hypoventilation if patient is on supplemental oxygen
Absence of constipation does not rule out opioid effect
sections.p: Serum drug levels are not routinely measured; normal vital signs do not exclude early respiratory depression, especially in the elderly.
